newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - Exports and S.Africa's rand - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Exports and S.Africa's rand - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
Inevitably, we are all prone to sweeping generalisations when it all seems so obvious.
Thus, there has been a general presumption, which it would have been foolish to contradict or question, that exports would expand as a direct result of the rand's depreciation last year.
It was evident in most commentaries at the time.

And the Reserve Bank, in its last Quarterly Bulletin, was able to explain that the 12 percent volume expansion of exports in 1996 was greatly assisted by the increased competitiveness of South African manufacturers in export markets owing to the weaker rand.
The same thought is fundamental to government's industrialisation policy as reflected, in particular, in the Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy document.

This turns on the accelerated reduction of import tariffs, which will enable domestic industry to overcome its export bias through the reduction in input costs. With reduced end-prices, it will become more competitive and hence expand exports.
Basically, it is very naive but, nevertheless, there is the notion which has gone unchallenged that with whatever reduction in end-price there will be an automatic expansion of sales.
Rand depreciation provides scope for an equivalent reduction in end-price in international markets and hence the opportunity to expand sales.
It has therefore been an easy step to suppose that the rand depreciation also provides an opportunity for a further acceleration of the liberalisation programme.

Before considering the merits of the arguments it is, unfortunately, necessary to cast doubt on the Reserve Bank's estimate of the volume increase in exports last year, and for that matter also for imports, which the Bank put at an increase of 10.5 percent in terms of quantity.
A completely different picture emerges when the 1996 monthly data for exports and imports as published by the Commissioner of Customs and Excise are revalued at constant 1990 exchange rates.
The real increase in exports corresponding to the notion of volume change emerges as only 4.4 percent for the year, while that for imports as only 2.0 percent.

But these calculations are rough and ready because of the not inconsiderable adjustments to the trade figures during the year which were made without having any regard to currency movements - for example, an adjustment to absolute January figures being made in July.
This would tend to give a downward bias to the derived volume changes on a rising exchange rate.

It is totally presumptuous to say the Reserve Bank is wrong in its figures, but given the awful mess it has been making of the gold export figures one can at least entertain serious reservations about the reliability of its estimates of unit values and volumes of foreign trade.

Reverting to the issue at hand, South Africa's exports could be considered as falling into two broad categories, namely exports for which the international price is determined on international markets and exports at prices offered by the exporter.

The former includes South Africa's mineral exports and much of the so-called beneficated metals and alloys. The volumes exported are dictated by international contracts secured or by the availability of supply from the South African exporters, for example, the volume of stainless steel or aluminium ingots produced.
These exporters are price takers in say, dollars, but the rand exchange rate is of crucial importance to them as far as profitability is concerned.

A recent analysis of 1995 exports shows that the mining industry directly accounted for 50.6 percent of total exports and a further 11.7 percent was attributable to the basic ferrous and non-ferrous metal industries, giving a total of 62.3 percent flowing from the exploitation of South Africa's mineral resources.

Virtually all of this is passive as far as pricing is concerned. Much of the agricultural products and the paper pulp exports would also fall into this category and they add a further 10.0 percent, giving an adjusted total for the first category of 72.3 percent.

The remaining 27.7 percent can therefore qualify for inclusion in the second category of independence of price fixing and therefore being able to take advantage of the depreciation of the rand in promoting exports.

These would all be in respect of manufactured products. But these exports, which are strictly for the South African Customs Union embracing South Africa, Lesotho, Swaziland, Botswana and Namibia, would include the bulk of of all re-exports as well as ordinary exports to African countries.
Indeed, a considerable part of total exports to African countries consists of manufactures that have been imported in bulk from other countries and then re-exported on a consignment basis.

As the exchange rates against the major trading partners on the African continent are fairly stable and certainly would not have been affected by the rand's depreciation last year, it would be fair to remove exports to African countries from the 27.7 percent second category.
This results in a residual 16 percent of total exports that might be considered as responsive to the rand's depreciation.
If only about a sixth of total exports is rand sensitive there is comparatively little to be expected from rand depreciation, even on the scale of 1996.

With total exports of 102 billion rand in 1995 there would be some 16 billion rand of exports possibly being affected, but there would certainly not be an increase in exports proportionate to the rand's depreciation.
Given the innate lack of competitiveness of South African industry, it could be a third of the currency movement at very best, which for 1996 would be about eight percent.
Thus the massive depreciation of the rand in 1996 might have at best accounted for an increase of 1.3 billion rand in 1995 values.
Any talk of a four percent depreciation being the equivalent of a one percent reduction in interest rates, as has come from certain quarters, is clearly grossly exaggerated for South Africa.
It might be roughly true of a mature economy like the United Kingdom, where most of exports are truly manufactures and competitive.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
